summary: This experimental memo describes the architecture behind the Group Key Management Protocol: how grouped symmetric keys can be created and distributed among communicating peers. The detailed protocol is in the companion RFC 2093.

plainLanguage.summary: The blueprint for how a club makes and shares its secret code, before anyone writes down the exact steps.

questions: how do groups share symmetric keys
how does group key management work
what is a group key controller
sender initiated vs receiver initiated multicast keys
subtitle: How a multicast group can make and share its own symmetric key without a central key distribution site.

tldr.problem: Secure multicast needs every group member to hold the same symmetric key. The usual way to set that up is a central key distribution center, which adds delay, a single point of failure and a juicy target.
tldr.mechanism: The Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP) hands key creation, access checks and distribution to the group members themselves. One member acts as group controller, builds the keys with a member, and passes them on to the rest, with peer review of permissions at each step.
tldr.outcome: This memo is an Experimental architecture. It lays out roles, scenarios and open questions rather than a finished protocol, and lists issues such as access control, error recovery and receiver-initiated groups that still needed work.

today: RFC 2094 is an Experimental memo, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It describes an architecture and lists open issues; it is not an Internet standard.

sections.title: What the GKMP Architecture Covers
sections.content:
This memo describes an architecture for managing the cryptographic keys of multicast communications. It names the roles and responsibilities of the system elements, sets security and functional requirements for each, and introduces the Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP).

The GKMP creates and distributes keys inside arbitrary-sized groups without a global, centralized key manager. It combines techniques used to build pairwise keys with the symmetric encryption of keys used by a key distribution center (KDC), and applies them to a whole group of hosts.

The authors say their work started in military command and control, where communication flows top-down and the higher-level party picks the members. They also looked at Internet multicast, where a receiver can ask the network to join a group without the sender being consulted. The aim is key management that supports both models, over circuit-switched or packet-switched networks.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is a blueprint for a way for groups to make and share their own secret code, without needing one big boss office to do it.

sections.title: Why Not a Key Distribution Center
sections.content:
Existing systems such as BLACKER, STU-II/BELLFIELD and EKMS (military) and X9.17 and Kerberos (commercial) use dedicated KDCs. A group key request goes to the KDC, which decides whether it is proper, contacts each member to download the key, and tells the requester when everyone has it. The memo notes this is faster than anything needing human intervention, but still needs set-up time, and a third party whose main interest is not the communication has to get involved.

Pairwise keys, by contrast, can be created by the hosts themselves with protocols such as FireFly, Diffie-Hellman or RSA. Those protocols rely on random information from each host and on peer review of permissions granted by a trusted authority, so key management becomes nearly invisible to users. The GKMP tries to extend that pairwise idea to groups.

The memo lists the benefits it expects over a KDC: more autonomy for key groups, lower latency to set up or rekey a group, less workload concentrated on one site, lower operating cost, less need for a high-capacity link to a central site, no single point of failure, and fewer people in the key distribution chain.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally one far-away office makes and mails out every club's secret code, which is slow and risky if the office is robbed. This plan lets each club handle its own.

sections.title: Sender-Initiated and Receiver-Initiated Groups
sections.content:
Both models assume a security manager that gives parties authentic identity and permission information. How that certification hierarchy is built is not addressed.

In the sender-initiated model, the originator gets a group management certificate that makes it responsible for the group key and gives its Group Key Management (GKM) application the membership list. The GKM application picks one member and creates a Group Key Packet (GKP) with it. It then contacts each member, checks the member's certificate against the group parameters, and sends a Session Key Package and a Group Rekey Package. The originator chooses the usage parameters and the member must comply, rather than negotiating them.

In the receiver-initiated model there may be no originator and membership can change minute by minute. One member is made controller, chosen by voting, by default (the first to transmit to the group) or by configuration. Only one controller may be active per group at a time. The controller builds the GKP with the first member who contacts it and keys later joiners as they arrive. For widely spread groups, regional key distributors can validate new members and pass them the current GKP; they do everything the controller does except create the GKP.

The memo says rekeying works the same way in both cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the group leader invites everyone and hands out the code. Other times people join on their own, so one helper takes charge of giving the code to each newcomer.

sections.title: Supporting Functions and Protocol Roles
sections.content:
The GKMP depends on two outside services. Security management covers network-wide permissions, secure start-up of the GKMP software on a host, and compromise recovery, including a Certificate Revocation List. Group management supplies the member list, group commands and role assignments, and receives progress reports. The GKMP deals strictly with cryptographic keys and relies on network management for addresses and for group address assignment.

Inside the protocol there are two primary roles. The controller starts key creation, forms the key distribution messages and collects acknowledgments. A receiver waits for a distribution message, decrypts and validates it, and acknowledges the new key. Every host can be a controller, which spreads the load and avoids single points of failure. Roles are binary: you are either the controller or a member, and an external entity decides which.

Only one controller should act at a time, since a group must share one key. The memo points out that having several hosts rekey a group simultaneously would be inappropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper is the key-giver and everyone else is a key-taker. A separate office decides who the helper is and who gets to join the club.

sections.title: Establishing, Rekeying and Deleting
sections.content:
Establishment has two phases, key creation and key distribution. A signed create-group command goes to the controller, which checks the signature and its own permission range. The controller then cooperates with a host to create two keys using software key agreement (the memo names Diffie-Hellman, FireFly and RSA) after verifying that partner's authorization. It distributes the keys only after checking each member's identity and permissions, and each member checks the controller too. If no suitable key exists between the controller and a member, a new pairwise key is created first.

Rekey replaces keys before their cryptographic life ends. It reuses an existing association, so identity and authorization are assumed. The controller creates new keys the same way, then sends them in a multicast message encrypted under the existing key encrypting key (KEK) all members hold. A token, signed asymmetrically by the group commander, shows that the controller is allowed to rekey and states the traffic level and rekey interval.

Deletion comes in two kinds. An administrative delete of a trusted member is a command, signed by the controller and encrypted under the group traffic key, saying to acknowledge and then delete the keys. Compromise recovery, for untrusted members, means building an entirely new group without them. The GKMP does not force a choice between destroying the group at once or running on until a new one is ready, but it can create a new group quickly. The compromised certificate goes on a signed CRL, which hosts check whenever a key is negotiated; group controllers are responsible for acting on it.
sections.plainLanguage: To start, the helper makes the code and checks each person before sharing it. To change the code, the helper shouts the new one using the old one as cover. To kick someone out, the club just starts a new code without them.

sections.title: Open Issues
sections.content:
Section 4 is a list of unresolved questions, not answers. It asks whether permissions handed down by a higher authority are enough for access control or whether more discretionary rules are needed, and how the protocol can police itself without humans or a central checker in the loop.

Other issues are running in a multi-level secure environment (where classification labels must match the operating system's labels), many more possible error conditions than with a pairwise protocol (messages may be delayed, lost or only partly received, and some errors can be induced by an attacker), and the gap between commercial and military needs, including cryptographic algorithms and how structured management is. For experiments the memo suggests using commercial algorithms with field sizes and delays that mimic the military ones.

For receiver-initiated groups it still asks who the leader is, how a new leader is elected, whether several leaders could appear, and how a new member could find a key source, for example through a broadcast the memo calls a Key ARP.

The security considerations section is a single sentence: the document, in its entirety, concerns security.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors admit they have not solved everything yet. They still wonder how to stop cheaters, what to do when messages get lost, and how to pick a leader.

items.label: Group Key Packet
items.desc: Holds the current group traffic encrypting key (GTEK) and the future group key encrypting key (GKEK).

items.label: Session Key Package
items.desc: A session TEK and a session KEK for one particular member.

items.label: Group Rekey Package
items.desc: The GKP encrypted in a KEK and signed with the controller's certificate.

messages.label: Create group keys
messages.note: Key creation, after checking the partner's authorization.

messages.label: Distribute keys
messages.note: Repeated for each member, after peer review of identity and permissions.
